findings.title: Legacy host values are copied without normalization and no longer match requests
findings.body: The migration inserts the old `embeddable_hosts` values verbatim using SQL, so entries such as `http://example.com` or `https://example.com/path` bypass `EmbeddableHost`'s normalization callback. Runtime lookup parses a request URL and compares only `uri.host` (for example, `example.com`) against the stored value, so these migrated hosts will never be allowed. The previous setting implementation explicitly supported scheme-prefixed values; upgrading such an installation can therefore disable all existing embeds until every host is manually edited.

findings.title: Migration crashes when the legacy embed category setting has no database row
findings.body: This dereferences `[0]['id']` from a query that returns no row when `embed_category` was never explicitly persisted or does not match a category name. A default/unused embedding configuration is a normal installation state, so the migration can abort before creating the replacement configuration. The fallback on line 14 is never reached because the exception occurs first.

findings.title: Host authorization fails for case variants of an allowed hostname
findings.body: The database expression lowercases the stored host but compares it to the unnormalized `host` value from `URI#host`. URI hostnames can retain input casing, while DNS hostnames are case-insensitive. Consequently, an allowed `example.com` can reject a request whose Referer or embed URL uses `EXAMPLE.COM`, breaking embeds depending on URL casing.

findings.title: Updating or deleting an unknown host returns a server error
findings.body: Both `update` and `destroy` use `where(...).first` and immediately call methods on the result. For an ID that does not exist, `save_host(nil)` dereferences `host.host` and `destroy` dereferences `nil.destroy`, producing a 500 instead of a not-found response. This makes stale concurrent admin edits and ordinary invalid resource requests fail as internal errors.

findings.title: Migration interpolates legacy host configuration directly into SQL
findings.body: Each legacy host string is concatenated into an INSERT statement without quoting or parameterization. A hostname value containing a quote will break the migration, and a maliciously crafted legacy setting can alter the SQL executed during upgrade. Values should be inserted through quoted/bound SQL or normalized `EmbeddableHost` records instead.
